question: Does a single treatment coefficient from pooled Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood with unit and time effects preserve the sign of heterogeneous proportional treatment effects under staggered adoption? Practitioners want one policy summary, but adjusting fixed effects can make an increase in a positive cell effect push the pooled coefficient downward.
result: The limiting population treatment coefficient β*(δ) has exactly the sign of Φ(δ) = MA − Σ_{g,t} D_gt R_g C_t. Here h_gt = π_g m_gt, R_g = Σ_t h_gt, C_t = Σ_g h_gt, M = Σ_g R_g, and A = Σ_{g,t} D_gt h_gt. Thus β* < 0 iff Φ < 0, β* = 0 iff Φ = 0, and β* > 0 iff Φ > 0. The stated conditions are multiplicative untreated means m_gt = B_gt exp(D_gt δ_gt), absorbing treatment, a fixed finite cohort set, T ≥ 4, adoption cohorts 2, 3, and 4 plus a never-treated cohort, no adoption in period 1, cohort shares and average baselines converging to strictly positive finite limits, treatment variation distinct from cohort and time effects, and δ_gt > 0 in every treated cell. The unit-effect population coefficient converges to this cohort-level coefficient. With a common treated-cell log effect δ₀, β* = δ₀ exactly.
mechanism: First, absorb each unit's baseline scale into its unit effect. Because units within a cohort share treatment paths and proportional effects, cohort means weighted by cohort shares preserve the population treatment coefficient. Fit these means by maximizing Σ_{g,t} q_gt[m_gt r_gt′θ − exp(r_gt′θ)], where q_gt = π_g/T and r_gt contains cohort effects, time effects, and treatment. To determine the treatment coefficient's sign, set it to zero and fit the fixed effects. Their scores match cohort and period totals, giving share-weighted fitted cells R_g C_t/M. Subtract their treated-cell total from the observed treated total A; the discrepancy is Φ/M and has the treatment score's sign. Concavity then determines which side of zero contains the optimum. To understand individual-cell influence, regress treatment on cohort and time effects using weights q_gt μ*_gt. The residual W̃_gt enters ∂β*/∂δ_ks = q_ks B_ks exp(δ_ks) W̃_ks / E, where E = Σ_{g,t} q_gt μ*_gt W̃_gt² > 0. Finally, recover untreated means as B^obs_gt = m_g1(m_∞t/m_∞1) and form PTT = [Σ_H q_gt m_gt]/[Σ_H q_gt B^obs_gt] − 1.
why_true: With a common effect, the fitted model reproduces every actual mean, so it recovers the common log multiplier. Under heterogeneity, fixed effects adjust when a cell mean changes; residualized treatment measures the variation remaining after that adjustment. A negative residual makes that cell's effect increase lower the pooled coefficient because every other factor in its derivative is positive. Globally, matching the margins supplies the fixed-effects-only allocation, and concavity converts its treated-total discrepancy into the coefficient's exact sign. PTT instead averages proportional effects with positive weights proportional to untreated exposure, so positive cell effects produce a positive aggregate.
example: Four equal-share cohorts adopt in periods 2, 3, and 4, or never, with untreated means equal to one. All treated multipliers are x except the period-4 cell of cohort 2, whose multiplier is y. The sign index is Φ = (5x² + 12x − 2y − 15)/16. At x = 101/100 and y = 4, every treatment effect is positive but Φ = −11559/32000, giving β* < 0. At zero effects, that exceptional cell has residualized treatment −1/8 and derivative −1/10, illustrating the local downward influence; the index establishes the large-effect reversal.
